Title: The network is back: Four questions for the AI era
Context: The firewall remains at the heart of the network as a critical source of threat context and enforcement, but effective network defense also requires visibility and context...
Full Text:
For years, applications, endpoints, cloud workloads, and identities took the security spotlight. The network — once the central pillar of cyber defense — drifted out of focus and out of the conversation.

But artificial intelligence (AI) is bringing the network firmly back to the table. As Eric Hanselman, Chief Analyst at 451 Research, part of S&P Global, put it during Sophos’ recent Securing the AI-Era Network roundtable: “The wire, the fiber. That’s truth, right?”

AI lives everywhere, but the network is the vehicle it must use to move within an organization. Every interaction between models, agents, users, and data navigates that infrastructure, giving the network a critical role in observing, controlling, and securing AI activity.

Sophos’ roundtable brought Eric Hanselman together with Sophos CEO, Joe Levy, and Dan Cole, SVP Product Management. This article shares their insights across four key topics to help your team spark discussions with the board about why securing the AI-era network belongs at the top of the agenda:

Speed and safety: Can security keep pace with AI ambitions?

Firewall scale: Can your firewall handle growing AI-era traffic?

Visibility, context, and control: Are your controls working together?

Vendor responsibility: What are vendors doing to keep products secure?

Speed and safety are no longer a trade-off

“Security must enable innovation rather than become the roadblock or the ‘Department of No.’”- Eric Hanselman, Chief Analyst at 451 Research, part of S&P Global

Whether through approved tools and services or unsanctioned shadow AI, the workforce will use AI. Security cannot stop that momentum, nor should it try to. Its role is to clear the way for innovation by managing AI use that creates unacceptable risk while securing the use cases that deliver real business value and greater efficiency.

For security to perform as the enabler of AI innovation and ROI, it must match the speed, scale, and scope of the technology it is protecting. Traditional architectures built around isolated tools, manual investigation, and delayed responses will struggle to keep up.

Instead, organizations need an AI-native security architecture that connects and correlates signals from across the network and other enforcement points and automates actions that do not require human oversight. This enables defenders to identify harmful activity and respond at machine speed without obstructing legitimate innovation.

Ask yourself: Today, can our security keep pace with our AI ambitions without slowing the business down?

Firewalls must scale without slowing you down

“You don’t want the firewall to become the bottleneck...[or] your single point of failure.”- Dan Cole, SVP Product Management at Sophos

AI is changing the demands placed on network infrastructure. A single user action can trigger numerous interactions between agents, models, data, and services, increasing the volume and complexity of network traffic. Organizations need to assess whether their existing firewall infrastructure has the performance and capacity to keep pace. The firewall remains at the heart of the network as a critical source of threat context and enforcement, but effective network defense also requires visibility and context beyond the traffic it sees directly.

Next-generation firewalls must be able to scale inspection without sacrificing throughput or resilience. This requires enough performance headroom to inspect growing volumes of encrypted, application-rich, AI-enabled traffic without becoming a pinch point. Firewall performance is part of the answer; extending visibility and detection across the network adds the additional context needed for a more complete defense.

That is where AI-native network detection and response (NDR) comes in. NDR complements the firewall by providing 24/7 surveillance across internal network traffic, detecting anomalous behavior and providing deeper threat context that the firewall and other control points can act on.

Ask yourself: Can our firewall handle growing AI-era traffic and inspection demands, and do we have the visibility required beyond its direct line of sight?

Visibility, context, and control are everything

“You’ve got to know more, correlate more, and pull that information together to make intelligent decisions about what you block and what you allow.”- Eric Hanselman, Chief Analyst at 451 Research, part of S&P Global

In the Sophos State of Ransomware 2026 survey of ransomware victims, 61% said their firewall detected the attack before the ransomware payload was deployed. Yet the attack still progressed to the point of ransomware deployment. The signal was there, but it did not lead to an effective response. It’s the security equivalent of the falling-tree paradox: if an alert fires but no response follows, does it really count as protection?

Visibility alone is powerless. Control without visibility lacks rationale. Combine both without context, and organizations risk blocking legitimate activity while leaving genuine attacks untouched. Without connection between visibility, context, and control, organizations are left with fragmented evidence rather than the connected defense they need.

The solution is to connect controls across the network, regardless of what or where they are, so that visibility gained in one place can inform decisions elsewhere. Those signals can then be enriched with shared contextual data to help each control point understand what it is seeing. From there, the appropriate control points can respond in coordination, turning distributed evidence into a more unified defense.

This forms a concerted, intentional movement. As Joe Levy said, “You have to have a cybersecurity strategy. It can't just be a collection of technologies that [you're] buying and then hoping for the best. You actually need to play this like a chess board and plan this thing out years in advance.”

Ask yourself: Are our security controls sharing enough intelligence to recognize and stop an attack together, or are we responding to threats in isolation?

Security vendors need to carry more of the weight

“We cannot continue to push the burden onto customers and say, ‘We gave you the patch; it’s your responsibility to apply it.’ The vendor has to bear that burden.”- Joe Levy, CEO at Sophos

AI is accelerating the discovery and exploitation of vulnerabilities, worsening an exposure challenge that defenders were already struggling to contain. As vulnerabilities emerge and are exploited faster, security vendors need to take a more active role in helping customers keep critical security infrastructure protected.

Vendors must take greater responsibility for protecting their products throughout their lifecycle. Customers need more than reassurance: they need clear commitments backed by verifiable actions and evidence.

In 2024, Sophos became one of the first security vendors to commit to CISA’s Secure by Design initiative. This continues to guide how we evaluate and improve our security practices. In a network security context, it means taking a more active role in protecting deployed firewalls throughout their lifecycle, from hardening and automatic updates to continuous monitoring for compromise. This does not replace the need for good network hygiene and timely patching, but it gives customers an additional layer of defense around technology that could otherwise become a threat actor’s entry point.

Ask yourself: What are our network security vendors actively doing to help keep the products we rely on secure?

The network security renaissance is an opportunity

The network’s return to the security conversation is not simply a technical shift. AI has not rewritten the fundamentals of network security, but it is making threats faster, more potent, and less forgiving of fragmentation and latency.

Bringing the network back into focus enables you to revisit the foundations of security and resilience, either independently or with the support of network and connectivity partners who understand this environment. It also creates an opportunity to reframe security as an enabler of AI adoption. By resolving the weaknesses that have held it back, organizations can move faster with AI, protect the use cases that create value, and tackle those that introduce unacceptable risk.

Title: Cooking with purpose: Giving our time to support families
Context: When your working lives are centered around protecting people and organizations, it’s easy to think about protection primarily in terms of technology
Full Text:
When your working lives are centered around protecting people and organizations, it’s easy to think about protection primarily in terms of technology. But sometimes, looking after people can be as simple as making sure there’s a warm meal waiting for them at the end of a difficult day.

Recently, a group of us from Sophos in Australia had the opportunity to spend a few hours volunteering through Cook + Connect with Ronald McDonald House, preparing meals for families staying close to their seriously ill or injured children.

It was a real team effort. We chopped, stirred, layered, baked and packed, with everyone taking on a different job in the kitchen. By the end, we’d prepared a spread of home-style meals including lasagna, chili con carne, chicken curry, salad, garlic bread and panna cotta.

For families focused on the care of a seriously ill or injured child, everyday things like deciding what to make for dinner can become another burden on an already overwhelming day. Ronald McDonald House helps families remain close to the care their children need, providing practical and emotional support through accommodation near hospitals, meals and shared spaces.

Knowing that the meals we prepared could offer families a little comfort and give them one less thing to think about at the end of a difficult day, made the experience incredibly rewarding for all of us.

Giving our time to make a difference

Experiences like this are something Sophos actively gives us time to pursue. Sophos employees can take up to 40 hours of volunteering leave every year, giving us dedicated time to contribute to the organizations, causes and communities that matter to us.

For us, that time is about much more than stepping away from our day-to-day roles. It’s an opportunity to put our values into action, connect with colleagues in a completely different setting, and use our time together to make a tangible difference.

Volunteering as a group also made the experience particularly rewarding. Working together towards something outside our usual roles gave us an opportunity to strengthen our connections as a team while contributing to an organization doing incredibly important work for families.

For me, experiences like this say a lot about what it means to work at Sophos. It's not just about the work we do. It's also about being part of a company that gives people the space to contribute to something bigger.

That’s increasingly important as AI gives attackers new ways to find vulnerabilities, develop exploits, and execute attacks at speed and scale. Sophos Endpoint is built around a protection-first approach that stops threats early, before they can escalate into larger incidents.

We’re excited to announce that Sophos has been named a Leader in the IDC MarketScape: Worldwide Modern Endpoint Security for Midsize Businesses 2026 Vendor Assessment (#US54834326, November 2026).

“Midsized organizations need endpoint security that can stop threats quickly without requiring constant tuning or specialized resources. Sophos Endpoint delivers strong upfront protection and integrated threat intelligence as part of Sophos Fusion, a cybersecurity defense system designed to strengthen security and reduce operational complexity.”- Mark Child, Associate Research Director, Security & Trust, IDC

According to the IDC MarketScape one of Sophos' key strengths is "Strong upfront protection across web, exploit, and ransomware vectors, validated across multiple independent testing programs, which reduces analyst workload and alert volume.”

Strong protection from day one

According to the IDC MarketScape, “Consider Sophos When: SMBs to large enterprises are seeking out-of-the-box, protection-first endpoint security with minimal tuning; organizations need a unified, open platform with strong third-party integration, native identity threat detection, and automation; and customers with limited security staff or no dedicated CISO function are seeking democratized, AI-augmented security and reporting."

Sophos Endpoint has recommended protections enabled by default, so teams get immediate protection without tuning individual applications, building exclusion lists, or keeping a security specialist on standby. It protects endpoints and servers across Windows, macOS, and Linux. As settings change over time, Account Health Check flags drift from recommended settings and high-risk misconfigurations, enabling administrators to fix issues with one click. Sophos partners can use one console to deliver consistent protection across small, midsized, and enterprise clients.

Block the techniques exploits rely on

AI can speed up exploit development, but it doesn’t change how exploits work on a device. Whether written by a human or an AI model, exploits still rely on a limited set of techniques.

Sophos Endpoint can block an exploit without knowing which specific vulnerability it targets or who wrote it. Its anti-exploitation technology targets the techniques exploits rely on, with 60+ proprietary mitigations enabled by default on every running process. We’ve been building and shipping this protection since 2015. To see how it works, watch how Sophos Endpoint stops exploits or read the Exploits Explained whitepaper.

Universal ransomware protection

Sophos Endpoint includes CryptoGuard, Sophos’ proprietary ransomware protection technology. Rather than trying to identify the ransomware itself, CryptoGuard monitors file contents for signs of malicious encryption. It blocks the offending process, whether it is running on the victim’s computer or on a compromised device elsewhere on the network (remote ransomware), and automatically restores encrypted files to their original state. Defenses that step up during an attack

When Sophos Endpoint detects an attack in progress, Adaptive Attack Protection instantly applies more aggressive protection on the device to disrupt and contain the attack. It responds to combinations of behaviors and the use of known attack tools, rather than relying on file hashes. That helps it respond to zero-day attacks and new variants, including AI-assisted attacks. Title: Proof-of-concept exploit code available for Ghostscript ‘Upload2Shell’ vulnerability (CVE-2026-125396)
Context: Sophos countermeasures SophosLabs continues to monitor the threat landscape for activity related to this threat and will deliver detections and protections as available
Full Text:
On November 21, 2026, pwn.ai described a proof of concept for exploiting a high-severity (CVSS 4.0 score of 8.5) vulnerability in Ghostscript, which is used to convert PostScript and PDF files into other formats. This use-after-free vulnerability (CVE-2026-125396) has been dubbed ‘Upload2Shell’. Attackers could exploit this flaw by sending custom PostScript or PDF documents that bypass the -dSAFER sandbox, gaining the ability to execute arbitrary code.

Artifex patched the issue in September, and affected distributions are being updated. There are no reports of active exploitation.

Recommended actions

Organizations should upgrade to the latest Ghostscript release as appropriate and can monitor the status of vulnerable distributions listed in the pwn.ai article. Until updates are available, organizations can reduce the risk by preventing Ghostscript from processing untrusted files.

Sophos countermeasures

SophosLabs continues to monitor the threat landscape for activity related to this threat and will deliver detections and protections as available.

The Sophos MDR team is actively monitoring for exploitation and post-exploitation activity related to this threat and will investigate and respond to suspicious activity.

An internal investigation is also underway to determine if Sophos products or services are affected.

Title: No Straight Lines: The value of a different career journey
Context: Since our Sophos Women in Technology (SWiT) No Straight Lines: Rebuilding and Rising in Tech event, I've been thinking about how much value people gain from the parts of their...
Full Text:
Since our Sophos Women in Technology (SWiT) No Straight Lines: Rebuilding and Rising in Tech event, I've been thinking about how much value people gain from the parts of their careers that didn't go according to plan. Career changes, time away from work, and moves between different industries can sometimes feel like things that need to be explained.

I think we should look at them differently.

These experiences can build resilience, curiosity, judgment, and perspective. They can change how someone approaches a problem or understands a customer, colleague, or situation. Those qualities matter enormously in technology and cybersecurity.

At Sophos, we talk about simplicity, empowerment, passion, innovation and authenticity. For me, valuing different career journeys is part of putting those values into practice. It means recognizing potential alongside experience. It means giving people opportunities to grow. And it means acknowledging that someone's career history doesn't have to fit a conventional pattern for them to make an important contribution.

Helping people see what they bring

The other important part of this conversation is confidence. Very few people build it entirely on their own. Having supportive colleagues, managers, mentors, and role models can help someone see strengths in themselves that they might otherwise overlook.

That's why communities such as SWiT matter. They create opportunities for colleagues to connect, share experiences, learn from each other, and realize that they aren't alone in navigating an unconventional path.

I'd encourage all women across cybersecurity and in the professional world to think about that in their own teams. Who might benefit from some encouragement? Whose transferable experience could bring a different perspective? Where could someone be given an opportunity to take the next step?

There is no single route to a successful career, and the more we recognize the value of different journeys, the stronger our teams can become.

Title: Empowering Employees to Make a Difference: The Digital Café
Context: So, I contacted my local volunteer office and launched “Digital Café”, a community initiative offering practical, friendly support to people who need a helping hand with...
Full Text:
Sometimes, making a difference starts with spotting a problem and deciding to do something about it. For me, that moment came around two years ago when I read an article in my local community newspaper about the challenges many older people face when navigating an increasingly digital world.

Using a smartphone, joining a video call, or setting up a tablet might seem like everyday tasks, but for people who are less confident with technology, they can become frustrating barriers to independence and staying connected with family and friends.

I wanted to help. So, I contacted my local volunteer office and launched “Digital Café”, a community initiative offering practical, friendly support to people who need a helping hand with technology here in Nauheim, Germany. On the first Wednesday of every month, we hold an open drop-in session at my local community center. Visitors can bring along their smartphones, tablets, laptops and apps, as well as any questions they might have.

No question is too small. Sometimes, my fellow volunteers and I help someone understand a new device or get an app to work. Other times, the impact goes much further. Recently, I helped a woman who had been struggling to get her tablet working again. Fixing the technology meant that she could video call her granddaughter again. It was a simple example of how digital inclusion can help people feel more confident, independent, and connected.

Giving people the time to make an impact

At Sophos, we believe that when talented people are empowered to do meaningful work, we can make a positive difference both inside and outside the workplace. Our company values include Simplicity, Empowerment, Passion, Innovation, and Authenticity, helping define how Team Sophos works together and the kind of company we aspire to be.

The Sophos Employee Volunteering program gives permanent employees around the world up to 40 hours of paid volunteering time every calendar year, enabling us to support causes that matter to us. With manager approval, that time can be used flexibly, including in one-hour increments, for individual or team volunteering.

For me, that means having meaningful support from Sophos to turn something I care about into action. I think “Digital Café” is a great example of empowerment in practice. I saw an opportunity, took ownership, and made something happen. It also reflects the passion our people bring to creating an impact, and the authenticity that comes from supporting causes that genuinely matter to us.

More than technology

So, why call it a café? Because solving technology problems is only part of the experience. While visitors wait, they can enjoy free coffee and cake provided by other volunteers. We want it to be a welcoming space where people can talk, learn and connect, helping to take away some of the anxiety that technology can create.

Alongside the Digital Café is the Repair Café, where volunteers help give broken possessions a second life. From household appliances and bicycles to children’s toys, the initiative helps prevent usable items from being thrown away while promoting sustainability and reducing waste.

What began as an idea I had on my own has now grown into a dedicated team of five volunteers. The Digital Café has become a trusted part of the community, welcoming regular visitors who know there will be someone there to help when technology becomes frustrating. It’s also exciting to see the initiative attracting wider attention. The mayor of Nauheim has taken an interest in what we’re doing, and I’m meeting with him to explore further ways we can support digital inclusion in the community. Our wider efforts have also included a “Cybercrime in Everyday Life” seminar for senior citizens, supported by a former investigator from the State Criminal Police Office (LKA) in Wiesbaden.

A culture that makes space for what matters

At Sophos, volunteering is one way we have the opportunity to make an impact beyond our day-to-day roles. The company’s volunteering policy reflects a commitment to the communities in which Sophos operates, as well as to employee health and wellbeing and a sustainable environment.

When I first read that newspaper article, I had no idea where it might lead. What started with an idea has grown into a community of volunteers helping people become more confident in the digital world. I couldn’t have done any of it without the support of the Volunteering Department in Nauheim.

Ultimately, the Digital Café isn’t really about smartphones, tablets, or apps. It’s about empowering people to stay independent, stay confident, and, most importantly, stay connected. I’m proud to work somewhere that gives me the time and support to make that difference.

Title: Introducing the new Sophos NDR
Context: As user behaviors are increasingly obfuscated by encryption and attackers are increasingly hiding their activities in ‘living off the land’ techniques, NDR will be critical in...
Full Text:
Attackers don’t need to compromise every security control; they just need to exploit a gap. As users become more distributed, applications and data spread across hybrid environments, and unmanaged and agentless assets proliferate, security teams face an increasing number of visibility gaps that attackers can exploit.

At the same time, AI is enabling adversaries to operate at greater speed and scale, accelerating established attack techniques such as credential compromise and vulnerability exploitation.1 This shift is already visible: Verizon’s 2026 Data Breach Investigations Report found that exploitation of vulnerabilities has overtaken credential abuse and phishing as the leading initial-access vector for breaches.2

Against this backdrop, the network becomes a critical vantage point for defenders, providing visibility into activity and behavior across the environment. Preventive controls remain essential, but no single control sees the entire attack. Network Detection and Response (NDR) helps close these visibility gaps by analyzing network traffic for suspicious behavior, giving security teams additional context to investigate threats, including across unmanaged and agentless assets.

Gartner’s outlook for the category reflects NDR’s growing importance: “The NDR market will continue to grow over the next decade, evolving from a niche security product to a critical one. As user behaviors are increasingly obfuscated by encryption and attackers are increasingly hiding their activities in ‘living off the land’ techniques, NDR will be critical in identifying both insider threats and threats that are launched from internally compromised hosts.”3

To address thes challenges, the new Sophos NDR gives organizations broader visibility across the network, active prevention capabilities, flexible deployment options, and network intelligence connected through Sophos Fusion.

Comprehensive network detection and response for the AI era

Originally introduced as an add-on to Sophos Managed Detection and Response (MDR) or Extended Detection and Response (XDR) in 2024, Sophos NDR is now available as a standalone solution.

What’s new in Sophos NDR:

Converged protection

Behavioral detection and Intrusion Detection and Prevention Systems (IDS/IPS) in one solution for known and unknown threats.

Dedicated Sophos NDR hardware

New purpose-built Sophos hardware for NDR workloads.

Active inline response

On dedicated Sophos NDR hardware, inspect traffic in real time and automatically block identified malicious traffic.

Available standalone

Purchase Sophos NDR as a standalone solution.

Deployment flexibility

Virtual, compatible third-party hardware, or dedicated Sophos NDR hardware, with passive and active inspection options.

Connected through Sophos Fusion

Centralized management, shared context, and coordinated response across Sophos Fusion.

“Network visibility provides an important layer of defense, particularly for devices and activity that preventive controls alone may not see. Sophos NDR builds on that visibility by combining behavioral network detection with active prevention and connecting network intelligence with context from across the Sophos Fusion defense system. This approach gives security teams greater context to investigate suspicious activity and coordinate response across the broader security environment.”

– Chris Kissel, Research Vice President at IDC

See more across the network

Known threats and unfamiliar attack behavior require different approaches. Signature-based inspection helps identify known malicious activity, while behavioral analytics help uncover suspicious patterns that don’t match a known signature.

The new Sophos NDR brings these capabilities together:

AI- and ML-powered behavioral analytics help identify suspicious network activity and unknown threats.

Encrypted traffic analysis helps uncover malicious patterns in encrypted communications without requiring full decryption.

Network analytics and threat hunting give security teams additional context to investigate suspicious activity.

Deep packet inspection and IDS/IPS capabilities add signature-based detection and, in supported configurations, inline prevention of known threats.

Together, these capabilities help organizations identify lateral movement, command-and-control communications, and unexpected data movement—including activity involving unmanaged and agentless assets.

This network perspective helps teams investigate activity that may not be visible to endpoint or firewall protection alone.

Stop threats faster: putting the “R” in NDR

A detection can tell you something is wrong. Active Inline mode adds the ability to act directly in the traffic path.

On a dedicated Sophos NDR appliance with the optional IDS/IPS Add-on, Active Inline mode inspects live traffic and automatically blocks known malicious packets before they reach their destination.

For organizations that want monitoring without enforcement, Sophos NDR also offers passive deployment modes. Customers can choose the approach that fits their network architecture and operational requirements.

Deploy your way

Network environments aren’t all built the same. Sophos NDR gives customers a choice of virtual and physical deployment options:

Virtual appliances for supported virtualized and cloud environments.

New Sophos NDR hardware, purpose-built for NDR workloads.

Compatible third-party hardware for organizations that want to use their own supported infrastructure.

Three traffic inspection modes provide further flexibility, depending on the hardware and configuration:

SPAN/TAP: Analyze a mirrored copy of traffic without placing the sensor in the live traffic path.

Passive Inline: Inspect traffic in the network path without actively blocking it.

Active Inline: Inspect traffic in the network path and block known malicious packets.

Active Inline mode requires a dedicated Sophos NDR appliance with the IDS/IPS add-on. Virtual appliances and compatible third-party hardware do not provide active inline blocking.

Network context. Coordinated defense.

Network evidence becomes more valuable when teams can connect it to what’s happening elsewhere. Through Sophos Fusion, Sophos NDR connects network telemetry, detections, and context with insights from endpoint, firewall, identity, email, and cloud security. This shared context strengthens Sophos MDR and XDR investigations and coordinated response.

Title: Physical Penetration Testing: When Physical Access Became Network Access
Context: Figure 1: Physical Penetration testing attack chain showing how public information, access control gaps, workplace trust, and internal technical exposure can combine, with...
Full Text:
This article is part of an ongoing series from Sophos frontline security specialists sharing lessons from authorized security testing engagements. Client information and selected operational details have been anonymized and generalized.

Physical security usually looks strongest from the outside. Cameras. Guards. Badge readers. Locked doors. Visitor procedures.

Each control may work exactly as designed. The harder question is whether they still work when somebody deliberately connects the gaps between them.

That is what a Sophos Physical Penetration Test is designed to examine. Rather than reviewing policies from a conference room, Sophos testers safely simulate an adversary attempting to enter a facility, move into sensitive areas, exploit workplace trust, and determine whether physical access can become digital access.

The following diagram shows the generalized attack chain assessed in this engagement, along with the places where alert employees, security personnel, access systems, network controls, and hardened devices can interrupt it.

Figure 1: Physical Penetration testing attack chain showing how public information, access control gaps, workplace trust, and internal technical exposure can combine, with detection opportunities at every stage.

The building was not the first target

The engagement started before anyone approached a door. The Sophos Red Team reviewed public information and studied how people moved around the facility. Public images revealed details about the property, its entrances, and the appearance of employee credentials. Onsite observation provided the rest: where people entered, how badges were carried, which areas were busy, and where an unfamiliar face might blend in. None of this required breaking a window or picking a lock.

A photograph shared for an innocent reason can reveal more than the person posting it intended. A badge image can expose its visual design. A building photo can show where reception sits. A normal workplace rhythm can reveal when entrances are crowded and attention is divided.

Individually, these details may appear harmless. Together, they can become a plan.

A valid badge does not always mean a valid person

Using information gathered during reconnaissance, the team demonstrated that access badge data could be captured and written to test credentials and cloned onto a fake badge. Those credentials allowed entry into parts of the facility and access to internal areas that should have required stronger validation.

Figure 2: Fake access badges created using badge data captured during reconnaissance, allowing the team to gain access to restricted areas of the facility.

Once a door accepted the credential, the environment largely treated the person carrying it as legitimate. That is an important distinction. A badge reader answers a narrow question: “Is this credential valid?” It does not necessarily answer the more important question: “Is the person presenting it authorized to be here?”

Employees encountered unfamiliar people moving through workspaces but did not consistently challenge them. Tailgating attempts also succeeded when people held doors or accepted a simple forgotten badge explanation. There was no dramatic confrontation. People were being helpful.

That is exactly why this type of penetration testing matters.

Inside, the trust boundary changed

After entry, the team identified unlocked workstations, unattended laptops, visible technical information, and gained access to internal network equipment. An authorized testing device placed beneath an unused workspace successfully established internal network connectivity.

Figure 3: An authorized testing device placed beneath an unused workspace.

That was the moment the engagement stopped being only a facilities issue. Physical access had become network access.

The assessment demonstrated that a person who entered the building could potentially reach internal systems without first defeating the organization’s internet facing defenses. The concern was not one specific port or one specific desk. The broader issue was that internal network access was being granted based largely on physical proximity rather than strong device authentication.

The team also encountered unattended and unlocked laptops in shared areas. These could provide an intruder with immediate access to applications, documents, communications, or a place to install persistence.

Once someone is inside, the workspace itself becomes part of the attack surface.

Encryption worked until another process failed

A test laptop provided another useful lesson. Full disk encryption initially prevented straightforward access to the device’s data. That control did its job. The team could not simply remove or mount the drive and read its contents. That's when the attack path changed.

Instead of attacking encryption directly, the testers evaluated the process used to recover the device. A believable support request resulted in the release of recovery information without sufficient identity verification. Combined with separate weaknesses in boot protection and privilege controls, that recovery information allowed the team to demonstrate a complete compromise of the test device.

The lesson is not that encryption failed. Encryption held. The recovery process around it did not.

Security controls rarely operate alone. Strong encryption can be undermined by weak recovery procedures. Strong endpoint protection can be undermined by insecure boot settings. Strong authentication can be undermined by a support process that trusts a believable story.

Some defenses did exactly what they were supposed to do

This was not a story where everything failed. The badge system generated alerts when cloned credentials were used in ways that did not match normal behavior. Security personnel raised their awareness, increased patrol activity, challenged a tester, confiscated the suspicious badge, and escalated the situation. Later attempts using invalid credentials were rejected, and additional security attention caused the team to abandon some entry routes. An employee disconnected the planted testing device, ending the team’s remote network connection. The employee may not have known exactly what the device was, but the action disrupted the attack path. These outcomes matter. A useful penetration test should not only document failures. It should identify the controls, decisions, and employee behaviors that interrupted the attack so those strengths can be reinforced.

The cheapest control may be a conversation

One of the clearest lessons from this Sophos Red Team engagement was that an unfamiliar person moving through a restricted workplace should not be able to rely on everybody assuming someone else has already verified them. Employees do not need to become security guards. They do need a safe, simple way to acknowledge unfamiliar people, offer assistance, and escalate concerns.

CISA’s “Power of Hello” guidance recommends observing suspicious behavior, initiating a polite conversation, evaluating the situation, and obtaining help when appropriate. Even a friendly “Can I help you find somebody?” can establish that a person has been noticed and may expose a weak pretext. Security awareness should make that response feel normal, not confrontational.

What organizations should take from this

This engagement was one anonymized example, not a claim that every facility has the same weaknesses. The broader lessons are widely applicable:

Protect badge information. Avoid publishing clear images of access credentials. Use badge technology that resists copying and limit each credential to the minimum areas required.

Require individual access. Employees, contractors, and visitors should authenticate or follow the visitor process rather than enter through ordinary courtesy.

Make polite challenges normal. Give employees simple language, a safe escalation path, and clear permission to report unfamiliar people or unusual activity.

Assume entry may eventually happen. Lock workstations automatically, secure sensitive documents, restrict internal rooms, and prevent unknown devices from receiving network access.

Harden recovery processes. Help desk and device recovery procedures should verify identity through trusted channels before releasing keys, resetting authentication, or granting elevated privileges.

Connect physical and cyber monitoring. Badge anomalies, visitor records, guard reports, network connections, and identity recovery events should contribute to a shared view of suspicious activity.

Test the whole chain. NIST guidance recommends structured security testing that includes planning, execution, analysis, and mitigation. Physical penetration testing adds value because it tests whether several individually reasonable controls can still be chained together.

The biggest lesson is not that organizations need more locks. It is that technology, process, people, and culture have to support one another.

A badge reader cannot challenge a convincing story. A locked door cannot protect an unattended laptop. Encryption cannot compensate for weak recovery verification. A network control cannot stop an unknown device if physical presence is treated as authorization. Layered security works only when the layers remain connected.

Title: ZDI-26-1030: (0Day) G DATA Total Security TSNxGService Link Following Local Privilege Escalation Vulnerability
Context: An attacker must first obtain the ability to execute low-privileged code on the target system in order to exploit this vulnerability
Full Text:
Vulnerability Details

This vulnerability allows local attackers to escalate privileges on affected installations of G DATA Total Security. An attacker must first obtain the ability to execute low-privileged code on the target system in order to exploit this vulnerability.

The specific flaw exists within the TSNxGService service. By creating a symbolic link, an attacker can abuse the service to delete a file. An attacker can leverage this vulnerability to escalate privileges and execute arbitrary code in the context of SYSTEM.
